atoms.text: This is an illustration of a witan, which was a group of important nobles and their king.
The witan came together to discuss laws and crimes at a meeting called a gemot.
atoms.sound: The witan came together to discuss laws and crimes at a meeting called a gehmot.

atoms.text: Early Anglo-Saxons had no written laws, so they relied on the decisions of the gemot being spread by word of mouth.

hint.label: Weregild
hint.text: Weregild literally means “man price”. It was a law that meant a fine had to be paid if someone was killed or injured.
hint.sound: Where guild literally means “man price”. It was a law that meant a fine had to be paid if someone was killed or injured.

hint.text: A feud was a long and violent dispute between families that often lasted for many generations!

feedback.finish: Damaging someone’s eye was costly, but injuring their leg or paralysing them at the neck cost more! Each finger also had a different value depending on its importance.

instruction.text: Select one of the holes in the wooden pillory to learn more about punishments in Anglo-Saxon society.

feedback.end: A pillory was designed to hold a criminal in place to embarrass them in front of the village. It was used for minor crimes.

instruction.text: Who do you think caught criminals in Anglo-Saxon England?

atoms.b: The law was ((++kept broken)) by the villagers using special groups called tithings, each consisting of 10 men.
The Anglo-Saxons did not have ((++prisons pillories)), so punishments included fines, having body parts ((++removed painted)) and even death!

text: In AD 600, King Aethelberht of Kent introduced the first written list of laws, known as dooms, and the specific punishments for breaking them.
